title: Paint Fence
statement:
A fence has `n` posts in a row and you have `k` different paint colors. Paint the fence so that:

- every post gets exactly one color, and
- no three or more posts next to each other share the same color.

Return the number of different ways to paint the fence; two ways are different when at least one post gets a different color. The inputs guarantee that this number is between 0 and 2^31 - 1.
constraints: The answer for the given n and k is at most 2^31 - 1
notes:
## Intuition

Trying all `k^n` colorings is hopeless beyond tiny fences. Instead, count the valid paintings of the first `i` posts, `dp[i]`, from shorter fences by looking at how the last post relates to the one before it:

- **Different** from post `i - 1`: take any valid painting of `i - 1` posts and pick one of the other `k - 1` colors, giving `(k - 1) · dp[i - 1]`.
- **Same** as post `i - 1`: then post `i - 1` must differ from post `i - 2`, or three would match. Take any valid painting of `i - 2` posts, give post `i - 1` one of `k - 1` new colors, and copy it onto post `i`: `(k - 1) · dp[i - 2]`.

So `dp[i] = (k - 1) · (dp[i - 1] + dp[i - 2])`.

## Approach

1. One post can take any of the `k` colors, so return `k` when `n = 1`.
2. Make `dp` with room for indices up to `n`.
3. Set `dp[1] = k` and `dp[2] = k · k`: two posts can never form a run of three.
4. For `i` from 3 to `n`, apply the recurrence.
5. Return `dp[n]`.

## Example 1, step by step

`n = 3`, `k = 2`. `dp[1] = 2` and `dp[2] = 4`. For `i = 3`: `dp[3] = (2 - 1) · (4 + 2) = 6`. Out of the 8 colorings of three posts only the two single-color ones are forbidden, so the answer `6` checks out.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): one constant-time step per post.
- Space: O(n) for `dp`; only the last two entries are ever read, so two variables would make it O(1).

## Pitfalls

- Two equal neighbours are allowed; only three in a row is forbidden, so `dp[2]` is `k · k`, not `k · (k - 1)`.
- With `k = 1` every fence of three or more posts is impossible; the factor `k - 1 = 0` gives 0 automatically.
- Handle `n = 1` before writing `dp[2]`, or reason carefully about a two-slot array.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `dp[i]` | number of valid paintings of the first `i` posts |
| `i` | the post being added |
| `k - 1` | colors that differ from a given neighbour |

narration.2: A single post can never form a run of three...
narration.3: ...so each of the k colors is one valid painting.
narration.5: dp[i] will count the valid paintings of the first i posts.
narration.7: Two posts: any pair of colors is fine, even two equal ones.
narration.9: Add the posts one at a time from the third onwards.
narration.10: Post i either differs from post i - 1 (extend dp[i - 1]) or matches it after post i - 1 changed color (extend dp[i - 2]); both have k - 1 color choices.
narration.12: dp[n] counts every valid painting of the whole fence.
